title: Fort Hood Shooter Seeks Court Halt to Pentagon’s Planned Firing Squad Execution, NBC Reports
body:
The U.S. military’s first planned execution by firing squad could be halted after the convicted former Army officer, identified only as the Fort Hood mass shooter, announced plans to file a constitutional challenge to the method and timing of his death. His legal team, speaking on Tuesday, said they will argue that the execution violates the Fifth Amendment’s guarantee of due process and the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment, potentially forcing the Pentagon to postpone the December 4 hanging of the 44‑year‑old who killed 13 fellow soldiers in 2020.

The case has revived a national debate that erupted last year when the Department of Defense disclosed a draft plan to livestream the firing‑squad execution for internal training purposes. Critics, including human‑rights groups, civil‑liberties advocates and several members of Congress, condemned the proposal as a “public spectacle” that would degrade the dignity of the condemned and could desensitize viewers to state‑sanctioned killing. Although the Pentagon later retracted the livestream idea, the controversy highlighted the broader unease surrounding the military’s reintroduction of firing squads—a method not used in the United States since 1961.

Legal scholars note that the challenge could test several unsettled areas of constitutional law. The Fifth Amendment’s due‑process clause has rarely been invoked in the context of military executions, which are governed by the Uniform Code of Military Justice and the Military Death Penalty Act. Meanwhile, the Eighth Amendment argument hinges on whether a firing squad—considered by some forensic experts to cause rapid death—constitutes “cruel and unusual” punishment in the modern era. The defense team also plans to raise concerns about the adequacy of the Pentagon’s procedural safeguards, including the selection of shooters and the secrecy surrounding the execution protocol.

Beyond the courtroom, the case is prompting policy makers to revisit the broader question of whether the United States should retain capital punishment for service members at all. The last military execution, that of Private John A. Bennett in 1961, was carried out by hanging. Since then, the military has relied on lethal injection for the few death sentences handed down, but a 2020 amendment to the Military Death Penalty Act reinstated the firing squad as an alternative when lethal‑injection drugs are unavailable. The Fort Hood case is the first real‑world test of that provision, and its outcome could influence future decisions about execution methods across federal and state jurisdictions.

Public reaction remains sharply divided. Victims’ families have expressed a desire for the sentence to be carried out swiftly, viewing it as a measure of justice and closure. Conversely, civil‑rights organizations argue that the execution, especially by a method reminiscent of 19th‑century warfare, sends a troubling message about the value placed on human life, even for those who have committed heinous crimes. The controversy has also sparked discussions about transparency in the military justice system, with calls for greater oversight and public reporting on capital cases.

If the courts grant a temporary injunction, the Pentagon will be forced to reassess its execution timeline and possibly explore alternative methods or further procedural reforms. Even if the challenge is ultimately dismissed, the legal battle is likely to set precedents that will shape how the nation administers the death penalty within its armed forces. As the December deadline approaches, all eyes remain on the federal courts to determine whether the firing squad will proceed as scheduled or become a footnote in an evolving debate over capital punishment in America.
